text: The central limit theorem is the reason so much of statistics works. It says that if you take many random samples and compute each sample's average, those averages form a bell-shaped distribution, even when the underlying data isn't bell-shaped at all. That's why a method built on the normal distribution can still be trusted on skewed data like order values, provided the sample is large enough. In this lesson you'll see it happen with your own eyes.

Take a population with mean mu and standard deviation sigma. Draw a random sample of n independent observations, compute its mean, and repeat many times. That collection of sample means has three properties: its center is mu, its spread is sigma divided by the square root of n, and as n grows, its shape approaches normal, whatever shape the original data had. Bigger samples give tighter averages, but the improvement follows a square root — four times the data only halves the spread.

Starting with a heavily right-skewed population — a million simulated order values from an exponential distribution with mean 40, skewness about 2.0. For sample sizes 1, 5, 30, and 100, we draw 5,000 samples each, average each one, and look at what those 5,000 means look like.

The mean of the means stays close to 40 at every single sample size — the center never shifts. At n equals 1, the standard deviation of the means is 39.26 and skewness is 1.81, basically the raw skewed data itself. At n equals 30, the standard deviation drops to 7.27, matching the predicted sigma over root n of 7.30, and skewness falls to just 0.4.

By n equals 100, standard deviation is 4.07 against a predicted 4.0, and skewness is down to 0.24 — the shape has become visibly symmetric, which the histograms show directly. A common textbook rule says n of at least 30 is enough, but that's only a rule of thumb — for mildly skewed data, 30 is plenty, but for data this skewed, some leftover asymmetry remains even at 30.

For extremely skewed data you may need hundreds of observations. A practical check: does a normal approximation at n equals 30 still give sensible coverage? Testing whether sample means land within 1.96 predicted standard deviations of the truth — which a normal would put at 95 percent — about 95.2 percent actually do. The approximation holds up decently even for this skewed data.

The theorem needs independent observations and a finite variance. Extremely heavy-tailed data, like the Cauchy distribution, has no finite variance, and its sample means never settle down. Strong dependence between observations — time series with autocorrelation, or clustered customers — also breaks the simple version. And the CLT is about averages; it says nothing about individual values, which remain just as skewed as ever.

To recap: sample means form a distribution centered on the true mean, with spread sigma over the square root of n, and a shape that tends toward normal as n grows. That's why averages are so well behaved, and why the next lesson can put an exact number on how far a sample mean is likely to stray — standard error.
